answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Wilde wrote the sentence in The Soul of Man Under Socialism, his long essay in the Fortnightly Review for February 1891. The wording above is the full original, individualist clause and all — it is the famous short version, not this one, that has been altered.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Soul of Man Under Socialism
Fortnightly Review, new series vol. 49, no. 290 (February 1891), pp. 292–319
59 autograph pages, dated 1890, the printer’s copy — Berg Collection, New York Public Library

source.excerpt: The wider sympathy is, of course, the more difficult. It requires more unselfishness. Anybody can sympathise with the sufferings of a friend, but it requires a very fine nature—it requires, in fact, the nature of a true Individualist—to sympathise with a friend’s success. In the modern stress of competition and struggle for place, such sympathy is naturally rare, and is also very much stifled by the immoral ideal of uniformity of type and conformity to rule which is so prevalent everywhere, and is perhaps most obnoxious in England.
trail: The essay ran in the Fortnightly Review for February 1891 ↗, and the sentence is there in the original magazine text, sitting directly after “The wider sympathy is, of course, the more difficult. It requires more unselfishness.”

An annotated bibliography of Wilde’s manuscripts ↗ records the printer’s copy — 59 pages in Wilde’s hand, dated 1890, now in the Berg Collection at the New York Public Library — and states that the differences between the 1891 magazine text and the 1895 private printing run only to spelling, punctuation, capitalisation and the dropping of the magazine’s italic emphasis.
The line survives intact in the book text as well: Project Gutenberg’s free e-text of The Soul of Man under Socialism ↗ carries the whole sentence, individualist clause included.
source.excerptNote: The two sentences before and the sentence after are quoted as they stand in the February 1891 Fortnightly Review text on Wikisource ↗.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Who was Oscar Wilde?
author.bio: Oscar Wilde, born in Dublin on 16 October 1854, became one of the most popular and influential dramatists in London in the early 1890s and is widely regarded as the greatest playwright of the Victorian era. Alongside the plays he wrote criticism and essays, of which The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891) is the most political — an argument that socialism’s real purpose is to free people into individualism. In 1895 he was convicted of gross indecency and sentenced to two years’ hard labour; he died in 1900, aged 46.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. The quotation usually is not — Wilde’s sentence has a hinge in the middle that almost every version online cuts out, and the clause that goes missing is the one that connects the line to the essay it comes from.

items.why: “Anybody can sympathise with the sufferings of a friend, but it requires a very fine nature to sympathise with a friend’s success” is the version on Goodreads ↗, with no work named and the site’s own note that community-added quotes are not verified. Quotefancy ↗ prints the same shortened text. The excised words — “it requires, in fact, the nature of a true Individualist” — are what make it an argument rather than a compliment.
A widely shared variant opens with “Anyone” and uses American spelling, as on Busted Halo ↗, which also drops the individualist clause. Wilde wrote “Anybody” and “sympathise.”
The Quotations Page ↗ names the right essay but dates it 1881. The essay appeared in February 1891, a decade later than that.

items.scope: A neighbouring line, not this one
items.why: “Whenever a friend succeeds, a little something in me dies” is a separate, much later remark. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to Gore Vidal, credited with a variant of the line — “Every time a friend succeeds I die a little” — in a February 1973 New York Times essay by Wilfrid Sheed, and using this exact wording himself in a September 1973 profile.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilde really wrote it — in the February 1891 Fortnightly Review ↗, and with the individualist clause in the middle.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence is not a stray epigram. It comes out of a stretch of the essay where Wilde is arguing that sympathy with pain is the easy, lesser kind, and that the harder task is sympathising with someone’s joy. He sets the line up with two short sentences — “The wider sympathy is, of course, the more difficult. It requires more unselfishness.” — and follows it by blaming modern competition, and English conformity in particular, for making such sympathy rare.

That is why the missing clause matters. “Individualist” is a technical word in this essay: Wilde’s whole case is that socialism’s point is to free people into individualism. Cut the clause and the line becomes a greetings-card observation about jealous friends; keep it and it is a step in an argument.
context.detailsSummary: The essay's own eventful publishing history
detailsBody: The Soul of Man Under Socialism first appeared in the Fortnightly Review in February 1891, pages 292–319. The manuscript bibliography ↗ records a first American printing in the Humboldt Library of Science, New York, in March 1891.

Its first appearance as a book came at a grim moment. Wikipedia’s account ↗ records the fifty-copy Chiswick Press printing of 30 May 1895, issued under the shortened title The Soul of Man — five days after Wilde’s conviction for gross indecency; the manuscript bibliography adds that it was privately printed for Arthur L. Humphreys. What was shortened was the title, not the essay.
